title: The hidden Christians of Japan
hookLine: after the Nagasaki martyrs, families kept the faith in secret, with no priests, for generations

lines: A MOTHER AND CHILD ON A SHELF.
cards: A small white figure of a woman holding a child sits on a farmhouse shelf in Japan. To a visiting official it looks like Kannon, a Buddhist figure of mercy. To the family who owns it, it is also Maria.
Christianity has been banned. Missionaries have been sent away, and on a hill at Nagasaki, Paul Miki and his companions were crucified for the faith.
Still, in fishing villages and on small islands, families went on praying. Quietly, with no priests at all. Children grew up, had children, and passed it on.

teach.b: Japanese has a name for them: kakure kirishitan, hidden Christians. Some historians keep that name for the groups who stayed apart after the ban was lifted, and call the families of the hidden years senpuku, underground.

First, the hiding. The faith lived inside ordinary households: a figure that could pass for something else, prayers said quietly at home, feasts kept without anyone outside noticing. Second, the laypeople.

With no priests, there was no Mass and no confession. But the Church teaches that in need, anyone with the right intention can baptize. So villages chose baptizers, and the water and the words kept going.
They kept a calendar of feasts, and prayers handed down by heart, called orasho. Third, the memory.
With no books in the open, prayers were learned by ear, and over the generations some words wore smooth, like stones in a river, a mix of Latin, Portuguese and Japanese sounds. Fourth, the return.

teach.h: OUR HEARTS ARE THE SAME AS YOURS.
teach.b: When missionaries came back and built a church in Nagasaki, tradition says a group of villagers came to the French priest there, Bernard Petitjean, and a woman whispered that their hearts were the same as his.
Then they asked him where the statue of Santa Maria was. Not every hidden community rejoined the Church; some kept the ways they had guarded so long.
In Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus tells his disciples: "Fear not, little flock." A little flock, kept for generations by nothing but memory.

how: Catholics in Japan keep the feast of Paul Miki and his companions, and pilgrims visit the churches and villages around Nagasaki linked to the hidden Christians.

games.q: you've kept the faith in secret all your life. now a new church stands in Nagasaki, with a foreign priest inside. what do you do?
o: stay away. it could be a trap.
go in, and quietly tell the priest your heart is the same as his.
write to the officials about the new church.
games.why: tradition says a group of villagers went in, a woman whispered that their hearts were the same as his, and they asked where the statue of Santa Maria was.

practice: Think of one small daily habit that holds what matters to you: a line said on waking, a sign of the cross, a thank-you before eating, something so small nobody else would notice.
If you pray, say a prayer you know by heart, slowly, the way those families kept theirs; if you don't, simply hold that small habit in mind for a while.

wordCard.voice: Kakure kirishitan. Japanese for hidden Christians, families who kept baptism, feasts and prayers alive in secret, without priests, generation after generation.

orig.note: Japanese: hidden Christians, the name for the families who kept the faith in secret.

carryVoice: Your line: 250 years in secret. A faith can live a long time on what a family hands down. Thanks for sitting with me.
